title: Zero-Rated on Paper, Taxed on the Invoice: GST/HST, QST and the CAD/USD Gap in Canadian Freight Billing for 2026
summary: How Canadian carriers and brokers get GST/HST and QST wrong on cross-border and transloaded freight, where CAD/USD timing eats margin, and what CRA checks.
body_markdown:
A Mississauga consignee's payables team flags a broker invoice in late October. The load ran from a plant in Ohio to a warehouse in Brampton. The invoice is in U.S. dollars, and it carries 13% HST on the line haul, the fuel surcharge and an unloading charge. The billing template defaulted to the destination province's rate because the delivery address was in Ontario. The broker's controller then finds the same template has fired on inbound loads for months.


The scenario is illustrative. The rule is not. Freight from a place outside Canada to a place in Canada is zero-rated under section 8 of Part VII of Schedule VI to the Excise Tax Act, so that HST was never payable and is not a sound input tax credit for the customer. The fix runs through the invoicer. Section 232 lets a supplier credit excess tax within two years of charging or collecting it, by credit note, and section 261 rebate applications carry the same two-year limit. Every month a bad default runs adds to the cleanup.


## The volume is steady, so the errors compound


Statistics Canada's preliminary leading indicator of trucks entering Canada (table 24-10-0059-01, released Nov. 12, 2026) counts 4,281,732 truck entries from January through October 2026. That is essentially flat against 4,284,972 in the same months of 2025, and about 4.7% below the 4,493,825 recorded in January to October 2024. Canadian-plated trucks made up roughly 87% of 2026 entries. Flat volume means growth will not paper over billing leakage.


## The tax map, by leg and by who is billing


CRA's GST/HST Memorandum 28-2, Freight Transportation Services, sets out a map most billing teams know in outline and encode poorly.


**International moves.** Canada to a place outside Canada is zero-rated when the consideration is $5 or more (section 6). Outside Canada into Canada is zero-rated (section 8). Outside to outside, including in-transit moves through Canada and in-bond freight not yet released by the CBSA, is zero-rated (section 9).


**Domestic legs of international moves.** A domestic leg of an outbound export is zero-rated under section 7 only if the shipper gives the carrier a declaration, in prescribed form, that the goods are being shipped for export as part of a continuous outbound freight movement, and the goods are in fact exported. A domestic leg of an inbound move is zero-rated under section 10 only if the supplier keeps documentary evidence that the leg is part of a continuous freight movement from an origin outside Canada to a destination in Canada specified by the shipper.


**Purely domestic moves.** Tax follows the destination. Under section 5 of Part VI of Schedule IX, a freight service is made in the province where the destination is. Per CRA's current rate table, HST is 13% in Ontario, 14% in Nova Scotia (down from 15% on April 1, 2025) and 15% in New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island. GST at 5% applies elsewhere. A multi-stop load with destinations in more than one province is split into separate supplies by section 136.3, each taxed at its own destination's rate. And per CRA, a shipment between two Canadian points routed through the United States is still taxable domestic freight.


**Quebec.** QST at 9.975% sits on top of GST, and its place-of-supply rule differs. Revenu Québec taxes Quebec-to-Quebec freight unless it is part of a continuous movement out of Quebec or from outside Canada. Freight from elsewhere in Canada into Quebec is deemed supplied outside Quebec, so no QST is charged, though a Quebec-resident recipient not using it exclusively in commercial activities must self-assess. For an export leg inside Quebec, form VD-197-V or the GST declaration supports zero-rating.


## Transloads, cross-docks and broken movements


Most disputed legs turn on whose instructions moved the freight. A "continuous freight movement" runs to a destination specified by the shipper, with every carrier acting on the shipper's instructions.


Take U.S. freight cleared at the border, cross-docked in Brampton and sent on to Moncton. If the shipper specified Moncton at origin and the Brampton stop was only a transfer, the Ontario leg and the Moncton leg can be zero-rated, if the carrier holds the paper showing it. CRA treats reload-centre handling as freight transportation where goods are not further processed. If instead the consignee took possession in Brampton and later tendered a new load to Moncton under its own instructions, that is a new domestic movement taxed at New Brunswick's 15%.


On outbound freight, "further processed, transformed or altered" before export breaks the continuous outbound movement. Kitting or relabelling at a transload is a question of fact to settle before the lane is priced, not after an auditor asks.


## Asset, broker and hybrid: who is the carrier?


Under Memorandum 28-2, a person need not physically move freight to be a carrier. It only has to assume liability as the supplier of the service.


**Asset carriers** billing shippers directly face the cleanest rules, plus one hidden leak: owner-operator chargebacks. When a carrier pays an owner-operator's fuel, repairs or permits up front and recovers them from settlement, CRA says those recoveries are consideration for supplies by the carrier and are not covered by the zero-rating for interlined freight. Unless the carrier truly acted as the operator's agent, it must charge GST/HST on the chargeback.


**Brokers that act as carriers** sit in the interline rules. Where several carriers take part in a continuous freight movement and one invoices the shipper or consignee, the supplies between carriers are zero-rated under section 11, for domestic and international moves alike, and only the invoicing party charges tax. That holds only if contracts, rate cons and invoices show the broker as the liable carrier.


**Brokers acting as agents** are on a different footing. CRA's freight carrier guidance says a freight forwarder arranging transport as agent for a Canadian shipper charges GST/HST on its commission whether the freight is domestic or international. The commission is zero-rated only when the agent acts for a non-resident who is not registered for GST/HST and the underlying freight service is zero-rated under sections 6 to 10.


**Hybrids** run both models, sometimes for the same customer, so treatment depends on which entity and role is attached to each load. That is a data problem before it is a tax problem.


## Accessorials do not get their own tax status by default


Charges the carrier bills its own customer as part of or incidental to the haul take the freight's status. CRA's examples include loading, unloading, storage, refrigeration and packing. Fuel surcharge is part of the price of the move.


The exceptions are where coding fails. Customs brokerage is a taxable service even on a cross-border load. Empty miles count as part of a freight service only when tied to a specific movement and documented. A pilot car supplied by a third party, or billed to someone other than the freight customer, is not incidental. Loss and damage settlements are generally not consideration for a supply at all. Section 162.1 deems demurrage not to be consideration for a supply, and whether a given truck detention charge falls within it is worth putting to your tax advisor rather than leaving to a default code.


## Currency: three documents, three rates


The rate con and shipper invoice are in USD. The Canadian carrier is paid in CAD. The gap belongs to whoever did not plan for it.


For tax, section 159 converts foreign-currency consideration at the rate on the day tax is payable or another day acceptable to the Minister. CRA Memorandum 3-6 accepts the day the consideration is paid, the day the foreign currency is acquired, or the average rate for the month tax becomes payable. Whatever method is chosen should be used consistently for a reasonable period, such as one year. The Bank of Canada, an accepted source, publishes one daily rate each business day by 16:30 ET, plus monthly averages.


The commercial exposure is larger. Bank of Canada data put USD/CAD at 1.3737 on Jan. 2, 2026, a 2026 low of 1.3515 on Jan. 29 and a high of 1.4271 on Oct. 9. It went from 1.3960 on Oct. 30 to 1.4257 on Nov. 13.


Run the numbers on one load. A broker bills a shipper USD 2,800 and agrees to pay a Canadian carrier CAD 3,700. At 1.3960 the revenue is CAD 3,908.80 and the margin CAD 208.80. Collected at 1.4257, revenue is CAD 3,991.96 and margin is CAD 291.96. Book it at 1.3737 on Jan. 2 and collect at 1.3515 on Jan. 29, and margin falls from CAD 146.36 to CAD 84.20, a loss of more than 40%. Nobody repriced anything.


Fuel surcharges add a second layer. A USD table indexed to U.S. diesel prices, applied to a Canadian carrier paid in CAD, carries fuel risk and currency risk on the same line. Asset carriers billing in USD with CAD costs are naturally long U.S. dollars. Brokers matching USD receivables to CAD payables carry the spread unless rate cons, invoices and settlements are tied to a stated rate source and date.


## What CRA is signalling for 2026 and beyond


No e-invoicing mandate has been announced. CRA's 2025-26 Departmental Plan (June 17, 2025) committed to evaluating how business-to-business e-invoicing could improve GST/HST compliance. That is an evaluation, not a rule. Budget 2026, tabled Nov. 5, 2026, proposes raising most fixed-dollar penalties under the Excise Tax Act and indexing them to inflation every five years, generally for reporting periods ending after 2027. The penalty for failing to file a return after a ministerial demand would rise from $250 to $1,000.


Documentation standards already bite. Under the current Input Tax Credit Information Regulations, documents of $500 or more need the supplier's name and registration number, date, total, tax or a tax-included statement, recipient's name, payment terms and a description of each supply.


## Encoding the rules


No two freight businesses draw these lines the same way. A reefer carrier running Ontario to the Midwest and a Montreal broker moving export freight to the port need different defaults, approvals and evidence.


Serious shops encode them. Tax codes by leg, origin, destination and role, not by the delivery address alone. Required document checks before a zero-rated invoice can be released: the export declaration, the original bill of lading or waybill. A currency set per customer and per carrier, with the rate source and conversion date stored on the load. Accessorial codes mapped to tax treatment, with customs brokerage and third-party pilot cars kept off the freight code. Permissions on who can override a tax code or issue a credit note, and an audit trail showing who changed what and when. The system should enforce decisions the business has already made with its advisors.


## FAQ


### Should a Canadian broker charge HST on a USD invoice for a load from the U.S. into Ontario?


No, a freight transportation service from a place outside Canada to a place in Canada is zero-rated under section 8 of Part VII of Schedule VI to the Excise Tax Act.


### Is the domestic leg of an export move zero-rated?


Only if conditions are met. The shipper must give the carrier a declaration that the goods are being shipped for export as part of a continuous outbound freight movement, the goods must actually be exported, and the charge must be $5 or more.


### What exchange rate should be used to convert a USD freight invoice for GST/HST?


The rate on the day tax is payable, or an accepted alternative such as the payment date or the monthly average for the month tax becomes payable. Bank of Canada rates are accepted; apply the method consistently.


### Do carriers need to charge GST/HST on owner-operator chargebacks?


Generally yes. CRA says recovered fuel, repair and permit costs are consideration for supplies by the carrier and are not covered by the interlining zero-rating, unless the carrier incurred them as the owner-operator's agent.
